The partition created a divide between Hindus and Muslims, leading to communal tensions that would echo throughout India's struggle for independence.

2. Official Secrets Act (1904): Enacted to curb the freedom of the Press.

4. Bengal Partition, 1905
Bengal was divided into:
1, East Bengal (Muslim) — At present: Assam and Bangladesh.
2. West Bengal (Hindu) — At present: West Bengal, Odisha, and Bihar.
Reasons given by Britishers for Partition of Bengal
The British justified the partition of Bengal in 1905 primarily on grounds of administrative convenience and the need to improve governance in a region with a large etc. and diverse population.
The actual reason was to "Weaken the Bengal" (the nerve centre of Nationalist activities).
Partition announced on: July, 1905.
Partition came into Force: 16th October 1905.
Reaction: Observed as a "Day of Mourning".
1905 Session of Congress
The Session happened in Benaras and was presided over by G. K. Gokhale.

The formal proclamation of the Swadeshi Movement (foreign made goods and products were to be boycotted) was made on 7th August 1905 in Calcutta Townhall.
1906 Calcutta Session of Congress
It was presided over by Dadabhai Naoroji.
Four Important Resolutions were Taken in this Session:
Swaraj as a goal adopted.
Boycott of foreign goods.
National Education (formation of National Education Council).
1907 Surat Session of Congress
It was presided by Rash Behari Ghosh.
In this Session, the Congress split into Moderates and Extremists.
Reasons for their Separation
The role of the INC in the manner of opposing the Partition of Bengal was the main cause of the Split.

The Extremists wanted the agitation to be a mass struggle all over the country. But the Moderates still had faith in the British administration and wanted to confine the boycott to Bengal and foreign goods only.
Britishers adopted "Carrot and Stick Model" within Congress.
Carrot: Appeasement to Moderates; Stick: Suppressing Extremists.
Methods adopted by Moderates were: Petitions, newspapers, pamphlets.

INDIAN COUNCIL ACT, 1909 ial
The Indian Council Act of 1909 is also known as Morley- Minto Reform. Lord Morley was the then Secretary of State and Lord Minto was the then Viceroy of India.
The provision for separate electorate for Muslim was introduced by Lord Minto (he is also known as "Father of Communal Electorate").
Viceroy Executive Council will have one Indian > First Indian to be a part of it was Satyendra Prasad Sinha.
Annulment of Partition + In 1911, Lord Hardinge I organised Delhi Durbar (3rd Delhi Durbar) for the coronation of King George V.
Key decisions:
1. Reunification of Bengal, announced by King George V.
2. The capital was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911.
Note:
—> Delhi Durbans have been organised three times:
1st Delhi Durbar (1877): Held under Lord Lytton to proclaim Queen Victoria as Empress of India.
2nd Delhi Durbar (1903): Held under Lord Curzon to celebrate the coronation of Edward VII.
3rd Delhi Durbar (1911): Held under Lord Hardinge II; during this, the Partition of Bengal was annulled and the capital was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi.

Komagata Maru Incident, 1914
+ A Japanese ship taken on lease by Sikh businessman and sailed to Vancouver (Canada) from Hong Kong.

Thisincidentinvolveda ship carrying 376 Indian passengers, primarily Sikhs who were denied entry to Canada due to discriminatory immigration laws. Forced to return to India, they faced further mistreatment, highlighting the struggle against racial discrimination and colonial oppression.
Defence of India Act 1915
+ This Act was enacted by the British government in India to suppress the Ghadrites particularly in Punjab, during World War I.
This Act was later replaced by a Permanent Act called Rowlatt Act.
In 1914, World War I began — It was fought between the Central Powers and the Allied Powers.

Belgium, France, Great Britain (and Commonwealth), Italy, Japan, Russia, and USA.
Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria, Germany, and Ottoman Empire (Turkey).
During the World War IL, in the context of the Indian nationalist:
The Moderates supported the war as a matter of duty.
The Extremists supported the war, hoping for future self governance in return.
While the Revolutionaries, saw the war as an opportunity to actively fight against British rule and seek immediate Independence through forceful means.
